div.head: Abt 77.1
div.ab: Gif hit þonne facne is, ef þær æt ham gebrenge, ⁊ him man his scæt agefe.
Gif hit þonne facne is, eft þær æt ham gebrenge, ⁊ him man his scæt agefe.
Gif hit þonne facne is, ef[t] þær æt ham gebrenge, ⁊ him man his scæt agefe.
Wenn es jedoch trügerisch ist, da bringe er [sie] wieder nach [ihrem] Heimathshause, und man gebe ihm sein [Brautkauf]geld zurück [von Seiten ihrer Sippe].
But if it is deceitful, then let him bring [her] back to [her] home, and let his [bride-price] money be given back to him [by her kin].
If however there is dishonesty, she shall be taken back to her home, and the money shall be returned to him.
If, however, there is any fraud, she is to be taken back home, and he is to be given back his money.
If there is deception, afterwards let him bring [her to her] home, and let him be given his money.

note.seg: Diese leichte Ehescheidung (s. d. Gl 5) nach altgerman. Brauche musste im 7. Jh. auch von der Kirche noch geduldet werden; Pol Mai II 390. Sogar noch im 10. und 11. Jh. besteht sie bei Durham; De obsess. Dun. hinter Symeo Dun. ed. Hinde 154 f.

In the 7th cent. even the Church still had to tolerate this easy divorce (see that word in Gl 5) in accordance with old Germanic custom; Pol Mai II 390. It still exists near Durham even in the 10th and 11th cent.; De obsess. Dun., appended to Symeo Dun. ed. Hinde 154 f.
þær ‘dann, in solchem Falle’ s. Wb
þær ‘then, in such a case’; see Wb
Nicht etwa ‘der Brautvormund die den Brautpreis bildende Viehherde’; (gegen Price). Ham steht auch sonst für das Vaterhaus der Braut; II Cn 73, 2; anders o. 31

Not, as might be supposed, ‘the bride’s guardian [takes back] the herd of cattle that forms the bride-price’ (against Price). Ham also stands elsewhere for the bride’s father’s house; II Cn 73, 2; differently above 31
reddatur ei pecunia (Gl Eheschliessung 5.g); nicht etwa ‘der Bräutigam zahle nunmehr Brautkauf bar statt fehlerhaften Viehs’; sceat bed. ‘Brautpreis’ 83. II Cn 74, ohne Ggs. zu Naturalien

reddatur ei pecunia (Gl Eheschliessung 5.g); not, as might be supposed, ‘the bridegroom is now to pay the bride-price in cash instead of in defective cattle’; sceat means ‘bride-price’ 83. II Cn 74, with no contrast to payment in kind
